Does Windows have a kernel? If so, why is it never discussed like Linux/Mac kernels?

You hear more about Linux's kernel than anything else because that's really all Linux is. "The Linux Operating System" is something of a misnomer. The "true" operating systems are the distributions: Debian, OpenSUSE, Fedora, Slackware, Ubuntu, etc. The primary way that these OSs differ from Windows is that these organizations didn't create their kernels; instead they all use the Linux kernel.

Back before Linux came about, there was (and still is) the GNU Project, which protested the closed nature of proprietary systems of its day and sought to create a completely free and open operating system from scratch. And they succeeded at creating every component they needed (most of the mv/cp/rm tools you might recognize from the cli), except one. The Big One. The kernel. Without the kernel, everything else is useless. Development of the kernel was coming along slowly for whatever reason. So the whole project was (and still is) stalled while they try to get that working.

Meanwhile, Linus started sharing his pet project on the intertubes: a Kernel. Just a kernel. Nothing else. Kinda neat, but it lacked any of the software that would make it a true operating system. So a lot of people that were tired of waiting for the GNU's kernel to be finished decided to port the GNU OS over to Linus' kernel. And that's pretty much how things continue to this day: Linus heads up development of the kernel, and people/organizations that are interested in building a Linux-based OS package that kernel up with whatever else they think their OS needs (GNU, init/systemd, X.org/Wayland, KDE/GNOME, etc.)

The gnu hurd project is moving foward after 20 years in development hell. The main obstacle was the micro kernel vs monolithic kernel decision. The choice to go with micro kernel will allow the hurd to skip some of the nuances and obstacles of the linux as the future comes and performance capabilities come into question. In theory, the hurd kernel could plug into the existing linux infrastructure with the wide range of GPL tools already made to run on linux.

Mac OS is based on FreeBSD which uses a monolithic kernel ie. it has everything you could need, it will take a lot more resources but it will work on wider variety of platforms without much effort. The Windows kernel is similar, it is designed to be more compatible over it being light.

Linux kernel or simply put Linux is essentially only the things you need. It was designed to run with the least amount of resources possible. You choose what features you want in it and generally nothing more. This is kinda reversed in distributions like Ubuntu where kernels are going backwards to the BSD/Windows way of supporting everything possible, which leads to it being heavier on the available resources. Naturally if you're not familiar with compiling your own kernels choosing Ubuntu might be easier.
